# Demographic, Lifestyle, Metabolic, and Renal Factors Associated with Blood Pressure in U.S. Adults: A Survey-Weighted Analysis and Predictive Modeling Study

> **Background:** Blood pressure is an important modifiable determinant of cardiovascular risk, with substantial variation across demographic and clinical characteristics. This study examined the adjusted associations of demographic, socioeconomic, anthropometric, metabolic, and renal characteristics with systolic and diastolic blood pressure, while evaluating the ability of these characteristics to predict individual blood pressure values.
>
> **Methods:** This cross-sectional study used NHANES 2021–2023 data from US adults. Survey-weighted descriptive and multivariable linear regression analyses were conducted to assess associations with systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Separately, ordinary linear regression, ridge, lasso, and elastic net models were developed for prediction using an 80/20 training–test split and repeated 10-fold cross-validation. Predictive performance was evaluated using RMSE, MAE, and R², alongside subgroup and residual analyses.
>
> **Results:** Age and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio were positively associated with systolic blood pressure, whereas BMI and pulse rate were positively associated with diastolic blood pressure in the respective final models. Female sex was associated with lower blood pressure, while non-Hispanic Black adults had higher adjusted levels than non-Hispanic White adults. Predictive performance was modest, with test-set R² values of 0.212 for systolic and 0.177 for diastolic blood pressure. Regularization provided negligible improvement over ordinary linear regression, and prediction errors varied across subgroups.
>
> **Conclusion:** Demographic and clinical characteristics showed different adjusted associations with systolic and diastolic blood pressure, but their ability to predict individual blood pressure values was limited. These findings highlight the distinction between population-level associations and individual-level prediction and support further research using additional predictors, flexible modeling approaches, and external validation.

## 1.0 Introduction

Blood pressure (BP) is a major modifiable determinant of cardiovascular disease and premature mortality [1]. Despite advances in prevention and treatment, hypertension remains a substantial public-health concern in the United States. During August 2021–August 2023, an estimated 47.7% of US adults had hypertension, and only 20.7% of adults with hypertension had their BP controlled to below 130/80 mmHg [2]. Understanding the demographic, socioeconomic, anthropometric, metabolic, and renal characteristics associated with systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) is therefore important for characterizing population-level differences in BP and identifying patterns that may inform further epidemiological research.

BP is associated with multiple interrelated characteristics, including age, sex, adiposity, glycemic status, kidney health, and socioeconomic circumstances. However, these characteristics may be correlated with one another, complicating the interpretation of their individual associations with BP. For example, body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference (WC) represent related aspects of adiposity, whereas urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) provide complementary information about kidney health. Moreover, associations may differ between SBP and DBP, making it important to examine these outcomes separately. Multivariable regression can estimate associations conditional on measured covariates, although findings from cross-sectional analyses cannot establish causal relationships.

A related but distinct objective is to determine how accurately a combination of these characteristics can predict individual BP values. Association analyses and predictive modeling serve different purposes: a characteristic associated with BP at the population level does not necessarily provide substantial additional predictive information, and good predictive performance does not establish a causal relationship [3]. Comparing ordinary linear regression with regularized approaches may also help assess whether penalization improves prediction when candidate predictors are correlated [4].

The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) provides population-based data on demographic, socioeconomic, examination, and laboratory characteristics, with survey methods that support appropriately weighted analyses of the US population [5]. Using NHANES 2021–2023 data, this study had two objectives. First, to estimate the adjusted associations of demographic, socioeconomic, anthropometric, metabolic, and renal characteristics with SBP and DBP using survey-weighted multivariable linear regression. Second, to develop and internally evaluate models for predicting continuous SBP and DBP using ordinary linear regression, ridge regression, lasso regression, and elastic net regression. Predictive performance was compared using repeated cross-validation, with additional assessment of subgroup errors and residual patterns. By addressing association and prediction separately, the study sought to characterize population-level relationships with BP while evaluating the extent to which the selected characteristics could predict individual BP values.

## 2.0 Methodology

### 2.1 Study population

This study utilized data from the NHANES, a nationally representative survey conducted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to evaluate the health and nutritional status of the civilian, noninstitutionalized U.S. population. NHANES employs a complex, multistage probability sampling design and collects information through demographic interviews, dietary assessments, standardized questionnaires, physical examinations, and laboratory testing. Survey data are released in two-year cycles and are publicly available for research purposes [6].

This analysis used data from the NHANES August 2021– August 2023 cycle. The included participants were adults aged 18 years or older who attended the Mobile Examination Center (MEC) and had at least one recorded SBP and DBP measurement. Female participants with a positive urine pregnancy test (n = 41) were excluded because pregnancy is associated with physiological changes that may influence BP and several study variables. The extended analytical sample was derived after applying these eligibility criteria and subsequent data cleaning procedures.

NHANES protocols were approved by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) Research Ethics Review Board, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants before data collection [7].

### 2.2 Inclusion and exclusion criteria

The study inclusion criteria included adults aged 18 years or older who had at least one measurement for their BP recorded during the MEC examination.

The exclusion criteria included participants younger than 18 years old, those with incomplete covariates, and female participants with a positive urine pregnancy test.

### 2.3 BP measurements

All BP measurements were taken in the MEC following a standardized protocol. Upper arm circumference was measured first to determine the appropriate cuff size. After participants rested quietly in a seated position for 5 minutes, three consecutive measurements of SBP, DBP, and pulse rate were recorded at 60-second intervals using an Omron HEM-907XL electronic upper-arm BP monitor. This device has been validated according to the standards of both the Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation and the European Society of Hypertension International Protocol for individuals aged 13 years and older. BP measurements were performed on the right arm whenever possible. The left arm was used only when contraindications or participant-reported conditions prevented measurement on the right arm [8].

For each participant, the mean values of available SBP, DBP, and pulse rate measurements were calculated and used in subsequent analyses.

### 2.4 Covariates

The analysis included a range of potential covariates from the survey that may influence BP or act as confounding factors: sex, age, race, income, education, marital status, insurance coverage, WC, BMI, pulse rate, presence of diabetes, glycohemoglobin level (HbA1C), serum creatinine (SCr), urine ACR, and use of BP-lowering medications.

Race/ethnicity categories were classified according to NHANES demographic variables and include: Mexican American, Other Hispanic, Non-Hispanic White, Non-Hispanic Black, Non-Hispanic Asian, and Other Race. The income variable is represented by the Family Income-to-Poverty Ratio (IPR), which is the ratio of family income to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services poverty guidelines, tailored to family size. Educational attainment is categorized as follows: less than 9th grade, 9-11th grade (including 12th grade without a diploma), high school graduate/GED or equivalent, some college or an associate's degree, and college graduate or higher. Marital status includes: married/living with a partner, widowed/divorced/ separated, and never married. It is important to note that NHANES has set top-coded values for age and IPR at 80 years and 5, respectively [9].

Furthermore, eGFR was estimated using the 2021 Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration creatinine equation without race adjustment to represent kidney function in the analysis [10].

The BP-medication variable had substantial missingness because the corresponding questionnaire items were subject to the NHANES skip pattern; only participants who reported having been told by a health professional that they had high BP were asked whether they were taking antihypertensive medication [11]. Therefore, participants who reported that they had not been told they had high BP were classified as “Not diagnosed,” rather than being treated as missing for the BP-medication variable.

Among these covariates, sex, race, education, marital status, insurance coverage, diabetes, and use of medications were categorical variables. The rest were continuous variables.

### 2.5 Statistical analysis

All analyses were performed using R version 4.5.3 (2026-03-11) within RStudio [12].

All analyses were conducted using a complete-case design. Data quality checks were performed before analysis. Variable ranges and extreme observations were examined using summary statistics, histograms, and boxplots. Potential outliers were manually reviewed against the NHANES documentation and retained when they were considered biologically plausible values rather than data-entry errors. Highly skewed variables were considered for logarithmic transformation before being used in regression analyses.

Baseline characteristics were summarized using weighted means and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for continuous variables and weighted percentages and 95% CIs for categorical variables. Sex differences were assessed using survey-adjusted Wald tests for continuous variables and survey-weighted chi-square tests for categorical variables. NHANES examination weights (WTMEC2YR) were used for measured clinical and laboratory variables [9]. Survey-design degrees of freedom were used for confidence-interval estimation.

### 2.6 Association analysis

Associations between BP and candidate covariates were initially examined using survey-weighted analyses. For binary categorical variables, survey-weighted t-tests were used, whereas differences across non-binary categorical variables were assessed using survey-weighted ANOVA. Multiplicity-adjusted pairwise comparisons were performed following ANOVA, using Tukey-adjusted p-values. Continuous variables were evaluated using survey-weighted linear regression, with log transformations applied where appropriate. Survey-weighted Pearson correlations were used to explore relationships among continuous variables, and a correlation heat map was generated to visualize the direction and strength of relationships among continuous variables, including BP measurements. Statistical significance was set at p \< 0.05.

Survey-weighted multivariable linear regression was used to evaluate the independent associations of demographic, socioeconomic, anthropometric, metabolic, renal, and treatment-related characteristics with SBP and DBP. A sequential modeling strategy was used. An initial demographic model included age, sex, race/ethnicity, marital status, education, IPR, and insurance status. Clinical characteristics were subsequently added to obtain the primary multivariable model, which included adiposity, renal function, and glycemic status, alongside the demographic and socioeconomic covariates.

Alternative model specifications were evaluated to examine the sensitivity of the estimated associations to the representation of clinical characteristics. These models substituted BMI for WC, log-transformed eGFR for log-transformed ACR, and HbA1c with categorical diabetes status. These alternative specifications were compared using model diagnostics, including the maximum variance inflation factor (VIF) and model deviance, in addition to the stability, interpretability, and clinical plausibility of the estimated associations.

Because the survey design provided 15 degrees of freedom, model complexity was constrained to support design-based inference. Race and education were represented using prespecified binary contrasts, reducing the number of estimated parameters and preserving adequate design degrees of freedom for survey-based inference. The resulting estimates were interpreted in relation to the specified reference categories.

Antihypertensive medication use was excluded from the primary model because treatment status may reflect prior hypertension and related clinical factors, and adjustment for treatment could alter the associations being estimated. Furthermore, including this variable increased model complexity and left insufficient residual design degrees of freedom for reliable design-based inference in the specified model. Given the cross-sectional design, medication-related findings were interpreted cautiously.

Pulse rate was also excluded in the initial primary specification because it was considered an additional cardiovascular characteristic rather than a core demographic, socioeconomic, anthropometric, metabolic, or renal covariate. Its inclusion was therefore evaluated separately to determine whether adjustment for pulse rate materially altered the estimated associations and model results.

Regression coefficients (β), 95% CIs, and design-based p-values were reported. Given the cross-sectional nature of NHANES, the estimated coefficients were interpreted as adjusted independent associations rather than definitive causal effects.

### 2.7 Prediction analysis

A separate predictive analysis was conducted to evaluate the ability of the available demographic, anthropometric, metabolic, renal, and cardiovascular characteristics to predict individual BP values. Unlike the preceding association analysis, which incorporated the NHANES complex survey design and sampling weights, the predictive analysis was developed without survey weights because the objective was individual-level prediction rather than population inference. All prespecified candidate predictors were entered into the predictive modeling framework, without excluding variables on the basis of their statistical significance in the weighted association models.

The data were randomly divided into an 80% training set and 20% held-out test set, with stratification by BP to maintain a similar distribution of the outcome across the two datasets. All model development and model selection procedures were conducted exclusively within the training data. The held-out test set was not used for model selection or hyperparameter tuning and was reserved for the final evaluation of predictive performance.

Within the training set, model performance was assessed using repeated 10-fold cross-validation with five repeats. The primary model-selection criterion was the lowest cross-validated root mean squared error (RMSE), with mean absolute error (MAE) and coefficient of determination (R2) also recorded to provide complementary measures of predictive performance.

Linear regression was used as the baseline predictive model. Regularized regression approaches, including LASSO regression (L1 penalty), ridge regression (L2 penalty), and elastic net regression (combined L1 and L2 penalties), were subsequently evaluated to improve prediction performance and address potential overfitting and multicollinearity among predictors. Hyperparameters for the penalized models were tuned using cross-validation within the training set, and the best-performing penalized specification was selected according to the minimum cross-validated RMSE.

The predictive analysis was deliberately restricted to main-effect linear specifications. No interaction terms, quadratic terms, higher-order polynomial terms, or spline-based terms were incorporated into the candidate models. A log-transformed scale was used when appropriate. This approach allowed direct comparison of conventional linear and penalized linear models while avoiding additional model complexity.

Predictor preprocessing was incorporated within the modeling workflow to prevent information leakage between cross-validation folds. Categorical predictors were converted into indicator variables, zero-variance predictors were removed, and numeric predictors were standardized before penalized regression. These preprocessing steps were estimated within the resampling framework rather than from the complete dataset.

The model with the lowest RMSE value was selected for refitting using the training dataset and then evaluated once on the untouched test dataset. Predictive performance was quantified using RMSE, MAE, and R2. Prediction errors were additionally examined using observed-versus-predicted plots and residual diagnostics. Residuals were defined as observed minus predicted, such that positive residuals indicated underprediction and negative residuals indicated overprediction.

Coefficients from the selected penalized model were extracted to describe the fitted predictive equation. Because these coefficients were obtained from a regularized prediction model, they were interpreted as predictive model parameters rather than inferential measures of independent association; therefore, statistical significance testing using conventional standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values was not performed for these coefficients.

Finally, to assess whether predictive performance differed across clinically and demographically relevant populations, test-set performance was additionally evaluated within subgroups defined by sex, race/ethnicity, BP-lowering medication status, and diabetes status. For each subgroup, RMSE, MAE, mean prediction error, and R2 were calculated. Residuals were also examined against continuous predictors – age, BMI, WC, ACR, eGFR, HbA1c, and pulse rate - to identify systematic patterns in prediction error.

## 3.0 Results

### 3.1 Demographics and Clinical Characteristics

Weighted percentages were calculated among participants with available data for each variable. The survey-weighted sample was approximately evenly distributed by sex, with males comprising 49.3% (95% CI: 47.8–50.7) and females 50.7% (95% CI: 49.3–52.2). Mean SBP and DBP were 121.2 mmHg (95% CI: 120.2–122.1) and 75.1 mmHg (95% CI: 74.3–75.8), respectively, and both were higher among males (p \<0.001). However, females had a higher mean heart rate (73.2 bpm, 95% CI: 72.5-73.9) compared to males (70 bpm, 95% CI: 69.1 – 70.8) (p \<0.001). Mean age was 49.1 years (95% CI: 48.0–50.2), with females slightly, but not significantly, older than males (48.6 vs. 49.7 years, p = 0.110). Males also had higher IPR (3.25 vs 3.00, p \<0.001) and WC (103.4 vs. 97.8 cm, p \<0.001). Whereas BMI was insignificantly higher among females (29.4 vs. 29.8 kg/m², p = 0.161).

Among participants, 63.3% were non-Hispanic White, 63.1% were married or living with a partner, 36.8% were college graduates or above, and 91.5% had health insurance coverage. Marital status (p \<0.001) and insurance coverage (p= 0.002) differed by sex, whereas race (p = 0.294) and education (p = 0.177) did not. Overall, 10.8% of participants had diabetes and 24.6% reported taking BP-lowering medication; neither differed significantly by sex (p = 0.189 and p = 0.805, respectively). Males had higher mean HbA1c (5.71% vs. 5.65%, p = 0.045) and serum creatinine (0.99 vs. 0.77 mg/dL, p \<0.001), while eGFR did not differ by sex (p = 0.850). Survey-weighted descriptive characteristics are presented in Tables 1 and 2.

```{r}
#| include: false

# ==== Importing data ====

# Give names for NHANES files
Files <- c(
   Alb_Cr       = "ALB_CR_L.xpt",
   Biochemistry = "BIOPRO_L.xpt",
   Body         = "BMX_L.xpt",
   BP           = "BPXO_L.xpt",
   BP_Qes       = "BPQ_L.xpt",
   Demo         = "DEMO_L.xpt",
   Diabetes     = "DIQ_L.xpt",
   GHB          = "GHB_L.xpt",
   Insurance    = "HIQ_L.xpt",
   Pregnancy    = "UCPREG_L.xpt"
)

# Get data from NHANES website  
Data <- lapply(Files, function(x) {
   read_xpt(
      paste0(
         "https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2021/DataFiles/",
         x
      )
   )
})

# Separate data into variables
names(Data) <- names(Files)

Alb_Cr       <- Data$Alb_Cr
Biochemistry <- Data$Biochemistry
Body         <- Data$Body
BP           <- Data$BP
BP_Qes       <- Data$BP_Qes
Demo         <- Data$Demo
Diabetes     <- Data$Diabetes
GHB          <- Data$GHB
Insurance    <- Data$Insurance
Pregnancy    <- Data$Pregnancy

# ==== Cleaning data ====

## ==== 1. Urine Albumin-Creatinine ratio (ACR) ====

# Rename columns 
Alb_Cr <- Alb_Cr %>% 
   rename (
      Albumin    = URXUMA,
      Creatinine = URXUCR,
      ACR        = URDACT
   )

# Selecting interested in columns 
Alb_Cr <- Alb_Cr %>% 
   select(
      SEQN, 
      Albumin, 
      Creatinine, 
      ACR
   )

## ==== 2. Biochemistry (Serum Creatinine) ====

# Rename columns 
Biochemistry <- Biochemistry %>% 
   rename (SCr = LBXSCR)

# Selecting interested in columns 
Biochemistry <- Biochemistry %>% 
   select(
      SEQN, SCr
   )

## ==== 3. Body ====

# Rename columns 
Body <- Body %>% 
   rename (
      Weight = BMXWT,
      Height = BMXHT,
      WC     = BMXWAIST,
      BMI    = BMXBMI
   )

# Selecting interested in columns 
Body <- Body %>% 
   select(
      SEQN, Weight, Height, WC, BMI
   )

## ==== 4. Blood Pressure (BP) ====

# Rename columns 
BP <- BP %>% rename (
   Systolic1  = BPXOSY1,
   Systolic2  = BPXOSY2,
   Systolic3  = BPXOSY3,
   Diastolic1 = BPXODI1,
   Diastolic2 = BPXODI2,
   Diastolic3 = BPXODI3,
   Pulse1 = BPXOPLS1,
   Pulse2 = BPXOPLS2,
   Pulse3 = BPXOPLS3
)

# Selecting interested in columns 
BP <- BP %>% 
   select(
      SEQN, Systolic1, Systolic2, Systolic3, 
      Diastolic1,Diastolic2, Diastolic3, 
      Pulse1, Pulse2, Pulse3
   )

## ==== 5. Blood Pressure medications ====

# Rename columns 
BP_Qes <- BP_Qes %>% 
   rename (
      Had_BP         = BPQ020,
      Taking_BP_meds = BPQ150
   )

# Selecting interested in columns 
BP_Qes <- BP_Qes %>%
   select(
      SEQN, 
      Had_BP,
      Taking_BP_meds
   )

# As these questions are only applicable for participant with HTN
# Use code "3" to code "Not applicable" group
BP_Qes$Taking_BP_meds [BP_Qes$Had_BP == 2] <- 3 

# Change 9 codes to NA
BP_Qes$Taking_BP_meds [BP_Qes$Had_BP == 2] <- 3 
BP_Qes$Taking_BP_meds [BP_Qes$Taking_BP_meds == 9] <- NA

## ==== 6. Demography  ====

# Rename columns 
Demo <- Demo %>% 
   rename (
      Sex            = RIAGENDR, 
      Age            = RIDAGEYR,
      Race           = RIDRETH3, 
      Marital_status = DMDMARTZ,
      IPR            = INDFMPIR, 
      Education      = DMDEDUC2,
      MEC_weight     = WTMEC2YR,
      Strata         = SDMVSTRA,
      PSU            = SDMVPSU
   )

# Selecting interested in columns 
Demo <- Demo %>% 
   select (
      SEQN, 
      Sex, 
      Age, 
      Race, 
      Marital_status, 
      IPR,
      Education, 
      MEC_weight, 
      Strata, 
      PSU
   )

# Change 7 and 9 codes to NA
Demo$Education [Demo$Education == 9] <- NA

Demo$Marital_status [Demo$Marital_status == 77 | 
                        Demo$Marital_status == 99] <- NA

# Absence of category "5" will lead to problems in interpreting
# results later on in modeling. Its better to eliminate this now
Demo$Race [Demo$Race == 6] <- 5
Demo$Race [Demo$Race == 7] <- 6

## ==== 7. Having Diabetes ====

# Rename columns 
Diabetes <- Diabetes %>% 
   rename (Diabetes = DIQ010)

# Selecting interested in columns 
Diabetes <- Diabetes %>% 
   select(
      SEQN, Diabetes
   )

# Change 9 codes to NA
Diabetes$Diabetes [Diabetes$Diabetes == 9] <- NA

## ==== 8. Glycohemoglobin (HbA1c) ====

# Rename columns 
GHB <- GHB %>% 
   rename (HbA1c = LBXGH)

# Selecting interested in columns 
GHB <- GHB %>% 
   select(
      SEQN, HbA1c
   )

## ==== 9. Insurance ====

# Rename columns 
Insurance <- Insurance %>% 
   rename (Insurance = HIQ011)

# Selecting interested in columns 
Insurance <- Insurance %>% 
   select(
      SEQN, Insurance
   )

# Change 7 & 9 codes to NA
Insurance$Insurance [Insurance$Insurance == 7 |
                        Insurance$Insurance == 9] <- NA

## ==== 10. Pregnancy ====

# Rename columns 
Pregnancy <- Pregnancy %>% 
   rename (Pregnancy = URXPREG)

# Selecting interested in columns 
Pregnancy <- Pregnancy %>% 
   select(
      SEQN, Pregnancy
   )

# Change 3 & 4 codes to NA
Pregnancy$Pregnancy [Pregnancy$Pregnancy == 3 |
                        Pregnancy$Pregnancy == 4] <- NA

# ==== Combine data ====

Data <- Demo  %>% 
   left_join (BP, by = "SEQN") %>%
   left_join (Insurance,by = "SEQN") %>%
   left_join (Body,by = "SEQN") %>%
   left_join (Biochemistry,by = "SEQN") %>%
   left_join (Alb_Cr,by = "SEQN") %>%
   left_join (GHB,by = "SEQN") %>%
   left_join (Diabetes,by = "SEQN") %>%
   left_join (BP_Qes,by = "SEQN") %>%
   left_join (Pregnancy,by = "SEQN")

# ==== Create derived variables ====

## ==== 1. Avg Systolic & Diastolic BP & Pulse ====

# Calculate average for systolic BP, diastolic BP, and Pulse
Data <- Data %>% mutate(
   SBP_avg = rowMeans(
      select(., Systolic1, Systolic2,Systolic3),
      na.rm = T
   ),
   
   DBP_avg = rowMeans(
      select(., Diastolic1, Diastolic2, Diastolic3),
      na.rm = T
   ),
   
   Pulse_avg = rowMeans(
      select(., Pulse1, Pulse2, Pulse3),
      na.rm = T
   )
)

# Convert NaN to NA
Data$SBP_avg[is.nan(Data$SBP_avg)] <- NA
Data$DBP_avg[is.nan(Data$DBP_avg)] <- NA
Data$Pulse_avg[is.nan(Data$Pulse_avg)] <- NA

## ==== 2. Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) ====

# Create a function to calculate eGFR using 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation
# eGFR = 142 * (min(SCr/k, 1)^ a) * (max(SCr/k, 1)^ -1.200) *
#        (0.9938^Age) * Sex_factor
# Sex factor = 1 in males and 1.012 in females

GFR_calculator <- function(SCr, Age, Sex){
   
   # Handling missing values
   if (is.na(SCr) | is.na(Age) | is.na(Sex)){
      return(NA)
   }
   
   # Determining the value of k, a, and Sex factor
   # Sex: males = 1, females = 2
   if (Sex == 1) {
      k <-  0.9
      a <- -0.302
      Sex_factor <- 1
      
   } else if (Sex == 2){
      k <-  0.7
      a <- -0.241
      Sex_factor <- 1.012
      
   } else {
      return(NA)
   }
   
   # Calculate eGFR
   GFR <- 142 * (min(SCr/k, 1)^ a) * (max(SCr/k, 1)^ -1.200) *
      (0.9938^Age) * Sex_factor
   
   return(GFR)
}

# Create a column for total weekly moderate physical activity
Data <- Data %>% 
   rowwise() %>%
   mutate (eGFR = GFR_calculator(SCr, Age, Sex)) %>%
   ungroup()

# ==== Exclusion criteria ====

# 1. Exclude < 18 years old
sum (Data$Age < 18)

Data <- Data %>% 
   filter (Age >= 18)

# 2. Exclude pregnant women

## 1 = positive results, 2 = negative results
table(Data$Pregnancy, useNA = "ifany")

Data <- Data %>% 
   filter (Pregnancy == 2 | is.na(Pregnancy))

# 3. Exclude missing BP data
sum(is.na(Data$SBP_avg) | is.na(Data$DBP_avg))

Data <- Data %>% 
   filter (!is.na(SBP_avg) & !is.na(DBP_avg))

# 4. Exclude missing covariates data

## Find number of missing data
map_dfr(
   c(
      "SBP_avg", "DBP_avg", "Pulse_avg", "Age", "Sex", "Race", "Marital_status",
      "Education", "IPR", "Insurance", "BMI", "HbA1c", "WC", "Diabetes", "ACR",
      "eGFR", "Taking_BP_meds"
   ),
   function (var) {
      tibble(
         var  = var,
         Miss = sum(is.na(Data[[var]]))
      )
   }
)

# Exclude missing data
Data <- Data %>% 
   subset(.,
          complete.cases(Data[, 
                              c( 
                                 "Pulse_avg", "Age", "Sex", "Race", "Marital_status", 
                                 "Education", "IPR", "Insurance","BMI", "WC",
                                 "HbA1c",  "Diabetes", "ACR", "eGFR", "Taking_BP_meds"
                              )
          ])
   )

# ==== Adjust categorical data variables ====

Data$Sex <- factor(
   Data$Sex,
   labels = c("Male", "Female"),
   levels = c(1, 2)
)

Data$Race <- factor(
   Data$Race,
   labels = c(
      "Mexican American", "Other Hispanic", "Non Hispanic White", "Non Hispanic Black", 
      "Non Hispanic Asian", "Other Race"
   ),
   levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
)

Data$Insurance <- factor(
   Data$Insurance, 
   labels = c("Not-covered", "Covered"),
   levels = c(2, 1)
)

Data$Education <- factor(
   Data$Education, 
   labels = c(
      "Less than 9th grade", 
      "9-11th grade (Includes 12th grade with no diploma)",
      "High school graduate/GED or equivalent",
      "Some college or AA degree", 
      "College graduate or above"
   ),
   levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
)

Data$Diabetes <- factor(
   Data$Diabetes,
   labels = c("No", "Yes", "Borderline"),
   levels = c(2, 1, 3)
)

Data$Marital_status <- factor(
   Data$Marital_status,
   labels = c(
      "Never married",
      "Married/Living with partner",
      "Widowed/Divorced/Separated"
   ),
   levels = c(3, 1, 2)
)

Data$Taking_BP_meds <- factor(
   Data$Taking_BP_meds,
   labels = c(
      "Not diagnosed",
      "Not taking",
      "Taking"
   ),
   levels = c(3, 2, 1)
)

# ==== Log variables ==== 

## ==== 1. Create log data ====
Data <- Data %>% 
   mutate (ACR_log = log10(ACR))

Data <- Data %>% 
   mutate (eGFR_log = log10(eGFR))

# Create look-up table
lookup <- list(

   Diastolic2 = "DBP: Second measurment",
   Diastolic3 = "DBP: Third measurment",
   Pulse1     = "Pulse rate: First measurment",
   Pulse2     = "Pulse rate: Second measurment",
   Pulse3     = "Pulse rate: Third measurment",
   Insurance  = "Insurance status",
   WC  = "WC",
   BMI = "BMI",
   SCr = "Serum Creatinine",
   ACR = "ACR",
   HbA1c     = "HbA1c",
   Diabetes  = "Diabetes status",
   Taking_BP_meds = "BP-lowering medications",
   SBP_avg = "Mean SBP",
   DBP_avg = "Mean DBP",

   eGFR = "eGFR",
   ACR_log  = "Log (ACR)",

# Create a for loop to plot histograms and boxplots, and calculate summaries
# for each column

Exploring_log <- function(vars) {
   for (var in vars) {
      
      Var_label = lookup[[var]]
      
      # Histogram with normal distribution curve
      Histogram <- ggplot(
         Data,
         aes(x = .data[[var]])
      ) +
         geom_histogram(
            aes(y = after_stat(density)),
            bins = 30,
            color = "black",
            fill = "lightblue"
         ) +
         stat_function(
            fun = dnorm,
            args = list(
               mean = mean(Data[[var]], na.rm = TRUE),
               sd = sd(Data[[var]], na.rm = TRUE)),
            color = "red",
            linewidth = 1
         ) +
         labs(
            title = paste("Histogram of", Var_label),
            y = "Density",
            x = Var_label
         ) 
      
      print(Histogram)
      
      # Boxplot
      Box_plot <- ggplot(
         Data,
         aes(y = .data[[var]])
      ) +
         geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
         labs(
            title = paste("Boxplot of", Var_label),
            y = Var_label,
            x = ""
         ) 
      
      print(Box_plot)
      
      # Summary statistics
      cat("\n", "Variable:", Var_label, "\n")
      print(summary(Data[[var]]))
   }
}

# Apply function
map(
   c("ACR_log", "eGFR_log"), 
   Exploring_log
)

# ==== Survey-weighted design ==== 

# Create survey-weighted design 
NHANES_design <- svydesign(
   ids = ~ PSU,
   strata = ~ Strata,
   weights = ~ MEC_weight ,
   nest = TRUE,
   data = Data
)

# ==== Survey-weighted descriptive analysis ==== 

# Function to return p <0.001 instead of 0.000
p0001 = function(x) {
   ifelse(
      is.na(x),
      "",
      ifelse(
         x < 0.001,
         "<0.001",
         sprintf("%.3f", x)
      )
   )
}

## ==== 1. Categorical Data ====

# Create a summarizing function to calculate: mean, 95%CI, and p value
weighted_Cate_summary <- function(var) {
   
   # Extract variable data
   x <- NHANES_design$variables[[var]]
   
   # Continue preparing variable data
   x <- as.factor(x)
   levels_x <- levels(x)
   
   # P-value
   pp <- svychisq(
      as.formula(paste("~", var, "+ Sex")),
      design = NHANES_design
   )$p.value
   
   ## Return summary as a table
   # Results container
   table <- list()
   
   # Table first row 
   table[[1]] <- tibble(
      Variable = lookup[[var]],
      All      = "",
      Males    = "",
      Females  = "",
      p_value  = pp
   )
   
   # Loop through variable's categories
   for (i in seq_along(levels_x)) {
      
      level <- levels_x[i]
      
      # Temporary design
      Temp_design <- NHANES_design
      
      # Create a dummy
      # 1 = participant belongs to this category
      # 0 = participant does not
      # NA = original variable was missing
      Temp_design$variables$Dummy <- ifelse(is.na(x),NA,
                                            ifelse(x == level, 1, 0)
      )
      
      # Extract males and females subsets
      Males_design <- subset(
         Temp_design,
         Sex == "Male"
      )
      
      Females_design <- subset(
         Temp_design,
         Sex == "Female"
      )
      
      # Calculate weighted proportion
      All_per     <- svymean(~Dummy, design = Temp_design, na.rm = TRUE)      
      Males_per   <- svymean(~Dummy, design = Males_design, na.rm = TRUE)
      Females_per <- svymean(~Dummy, design = Females_design, na.rm = TRUE)
      
      # Table's rest rows 
      table[[i + 1]] <- tibble(
         Variable = level,
         All      = sprintf(
            "%.1f (%.1f - %.1f)",
            coef(All_per) * 100,
            confint(All_per)[, 1] * 100,
            confint(All_per)[, 2] * 100
         ),
         
         Males    = sprintf(
            "%.1f (%.1f - %.1f)",
            coef(Males_per) * 100,
            confint(Males_per)[, 1] * 100,
            confint(Males_per)[, 2] * 100
         ),
         
         Females  = sprintf(
            "%.1f (%.1f - %.1f)",
            coef(Females_per) * 100,
            confint(Females_per)[, 1] * 100,
            confint(Females_per)[, 2] * 100
         ),
         
         p_value  = NA_real_
      )
   }
   
   bind_rows(table)
}

# Apply function and print table in a tidy way
weighted_cate <- map_dfr(
   c(
      "Race", "Marital_status", "Education", "Insurance", 
      "Taking_BP_meds", "Diabetes"
   ),
   weighted_Cate_summary
)%>%
   gt() %>%
   tab_style(
      style = cell_text(indent = px(20)),
      locations = cells_body(
         rows = All != ""
      )
   ) %>%
   fmt(
      columns = p_value,
      fns = p0001) %>%
   tab_header(
      title = md(
         "Table 1: Summary of baseline categorical characteristics"
      )
   )%>%
   cols_label(
      All     = "Total Sample",
      Males   = "Males",
      Females = "Females",
      p_value = "P-value"
   ) %>%
   tab_footnote(
      footnote = "P-values compare the proportion of each covariate between males and females using survey-weighted Chi square.",
      locations = cells_column_labels(columns = p_value)
   ) %>%
   tab_source_note(
      source_note = md(
         "Percentages and 95% CIs are survey-weighted."
      )
   )

## ==== 2. Continuous Data ====

# Create a summarizing function to calculate: mean, 95%CI, and p value
weighted_Cont_summary <- function(var){
   
   # Extract variable
   x <- NHANES_design$variables[[var]]
   
   # Extract males and females subsets
   Males_design <- subset(
      NHANES_design,
      Sex == "Male"
   )
   
   Females_design <- subset(
      NHANES_design,
      Sex == "Female"
   )
   
   # Create a formula
   formula <- as.formula(paste0("~", var))
   
   # Calculate means
   All_mean     <- svymean(formula, NHANES_design, na.rm = TRUE)
   Males_mean   <- svymean(formula, Males_design, na.rm = TRUE)
   Females_mean <- svymean(formula, Females_design, na.rm = TRUE)
   
   
   # P-value
   pp <- svyglm(
      as.formula(paste0(var, " ~ Sex")),
      design = NHANES_design
   )
   
   # Return summary as a table
   table <- tibble(
      Variable = lookup[[var]],
      All      = sprintf(
         "%.2f (%.2f - %.2f)",
         coef(All_mean),
         confint(
            All_mean,
            df = degf(NHANES_design)
         )[, 1],  
         confint(
            All_mean,
            df = degf(NHANES_design)
         )[, 2]
      ),
      
      Males    = sprintf(
         "%.2f (%.2f - %.2f)",
         coef(
            Males_mean,
            df = degf(NHANES_design)
         ),
         confint(
            Males_mean,
            df = degf(NHANES_design)
         )[, 1],  
         confint(
            Males_mean,
            df = degf(NHANES_design)
         )[, 2]
      ),
      
      Females  = sprintf(
         "%.2f (%.2f - %.2f)",
         coef(Females_mean),
         confint(
            Females_mean,
            df = degf(NHANES_design)
         )[, 1],  
         confint(
            Females_mean,
            df = degf(NHANES_design)
         )[, 2]
      ),
      
      p_value  = regTermTest(pp, ~ Sex)$p
   )
   
   table
}

# Apply function and print table in a tidy way
weighted_cont <- map_dfr(
   c(
      "SBP_avg", "DBP_avg", "Pulse_avg", "Age", "IPR", "WC",
      "BMI", "HbA1c", "ACR", "SCr", "eGFR"
   ), 
   weighted_Cont_summary
) %>%
   gt() %>%
   fmt(
      columns = p_value,
      fns = p0001) %>%
   tab_header(
      title = md(
         "Table 2: Summary of baseline continuous characteristics"
      )
   )%>%
   cols_label(
      All     = "Total Sample",
      Males   = "Males",
      Females = "Females",
      p_value = "P-value"
   ) %>%
   tab_footnote(
      footnote = "P-values are from survey-adjusted Wald test comparing males and females.",
      locations = cells_column_labels(columns = p_value)
   ) %>%
   tab_source_note(
      source_note = md(
         "Means are presented as survey-weighted mean (95% CIs)."
      )
   )
```

### 3.2 Relationship between BP and covariates

#### 3.2.1 Relationship with categorical covariates

Survey-weighted comparisons demonstrated significant differences in SBP across race groups (overall p = 0.013). In Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons, SBP was significantly lower among Mexican American participants than among non-Hispanic Black participants (−5.85 mmHg, 95% CI: −10.75 to −0.95, p = 0.018) and lower among non-Hispanic Black participants than among non-Hispanic Asian participants by 6.89 mmHg (95% CI: 0.19 to 13.59, p = 0.043). The remaining pairwise comparisons were not statistically significant after Tukey adjustment.

For DBP, race was also significantly associated with BP overall (p = 0.006). Tukey-adjusted comparisons showed lower DBP among Mexican American participants compared with non-Hispanic Black participants (−5.00 mmHg, 95% CI: −8.55 to −1.45, p = 0.006), lower DBP among other Hispanic participants compared with non-Hispanic Black participants (−4.20 mmHg, 95% CI: −7.38 to −1.01, p = 0.010), and lower DBP among non-Hispanic White participants compared with non-Hispanic Black participants (−3.60 mmHg, 95% CI: −6.03 to −1.18, p = 0.004). Non-Hispanic Black participants also had higher DBP than participants classified as other race (3.51 mmHg, 95% CI: 0.06 to 6.97, p = 0.045). Other pairwise comparisons were not statistically significant. Figure 2 illustrates the distribution of weighted mean SBP and DBP with 95% confidence intervals across race groups.

```{r}
#| include: false

# ==== Weighted ANOVA ==== 

# Create a function to perform ANOVA (plus post-hoc) and return results as a table
wt_ANOVA <- function(BP, vars) {
   
   # Create empty table
   Results <- tibble()
   
   for (var in vars) {
      
      Var_label <- lookup [[var]]
      
      # Create formulas
      formula1 <- as.formula(
         paste0(BP, "_avg~", var)
      )
      
      formula2 <- as.formula(
         paste0("~", var)
      )
      
      # Weighted ANOVA
      Model <- svyglm(formula1, design = NHANES_design)
      
      # Estimated marginal means
      Emm <- emmeans(Model, formula2)
      
      # Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons
      Pair <- pairs(Emm, adjust = "tukey")
      
      # Overall P-value 
      ANV <- regTermTest(Model, formula2)
      
      # Create separated tables
      table_1 <- tibble (
         contrast = Var_label,
         overall = as.numeric(ANV$p),
         B = NA,
         adj.p.value =NA
      )
      
      if (ANV$p < 0.05) {
         
         table_2 <- tidy(Pair, conf.int = TRUE) %>% 
            mutate(
               B = sprintf(
                  "%.3f (%.3f - %.3f)",
                  estimate,
                  conf.low,
                  conf.high
               ),
               overall = NA
            ) %>% 
            select(c(contrast, overall, B, adj.p.value))
         
      } else {
         
         table_2 <- tibble()
      }
      
      # Combine tables as one
      Results <- bind_rows(Results, table_1, table_2)
   }
   
   # Retrun results in a tidy way
   Results %>% 
      gt() %>%
      fmt(
         columns = c(overall, adj.p.value),
         fns = p0001
      ) %>%
      cols_label(
         contrast = "Variable",
         overall  = "Overall p-value",
         B        = "Mean difference (95% CI)",
         adj.p.value = "Tukey-adjusted P-value"
      ) %>%
      sub_missing(
         columns = c(B, overall, adj.p.value),
         missing_text = ""
      ) %>%
      tab_style(
         style = cell_text(indent = px(15)),
         locations = cells_body(
            columns = contrast,
            rows = !contrast %in% c(
               "Race",
               "Marital status",
               "Education level",
               "Diabetes",
               "BP-lowering medications"
            )
         )
      ) %>%
      tab_style(
         style = cell_borders(
            sides = c("bottom", "left", "right"),
            color = "transparent",
            weight = px(0)
         ),
         locations = cells_body(
            rows = contrast %in% c(
               "Race",
               "Marital status",
               "Education level",
               "Diabetes",
               "BP-lowering medication"
            )
         )
      ) %>%
      tab_footnote(
         footnote = "Overall p-values compare all subgroups using survey-weighted ANOVA.",
         locations = cells_column_labels(columns = overall)
      )  %>%
      tab_footnote(
         footnote = " Tukey-adjusted pairwise p-values based on comparisons between subgroups.",
         locations = cells_column_labels(columns = adj.p.value)
      )
}

# Apply function for SBP
ANOVA_SBP <- wt_ANOVA(
   "SBP",
   c(
      "Race",
      "Marital_status",
      "Education",
      "Diabetes",
      "Taking_BP_meds"
   )
) %>%
   tab_header(
      title = md(
         "Table 3: Survey-weighted comparisons of non-binary categorical variables for SBP"
      )
   )

# Apply function for DBP
ANOVA_DBP <- wt_ANOVA(
   "DBP",
   c(
      "Race",
      "Marital_status",
      "Education",
      "Diabetes",
      "Taking_BP_meds"
   )
) %>%
   tab_header(
      title = md(
         "Table 4: Survey-weighted comparisons of non-binary categorical variables for DBP"
      )
   )

# ==== Descriptive plots for categorical data ==== 

# Create a function to plot weighted BP mean (with 95% CI) across covariates groups
plot_categorical <- function(var) {
   
   SBP_formula <- as.formula("~SBP_avg")
   
   DBP_formula <- as.formula("~DBP_avg")
   
   var_formula <- as.formula(
      paste0("~", var)
   )
   
   SBP_by <- svyby(
      SBP_formula, 
      var_formula,
      design = NHANES_design,
      FUN = svymean,
      na.rm = TRUE
   )
   
   DBP_by <- svyby(
      DBP_formula,
      var_formula,
      design = NHANES_design,
      FUN = svymean,
      na.rm = TRUE
   )
   
   # Convert SE into 95% CI
   SBP_by <- SBP_by %>%
      rename(BP_avg = SBP_avg) %>%
      mutate(
         CI_lower = BP_avg - 1.96 * se,
         CI_upper = BP_avg + 1.96 * se,
         BP_type = "SBP"
      )
   
   DBP_by <- DBP_by %>%
      rename(BP_avg = DBP_avg) %>%
      mutate(
         CI_lower = BP_avg - 1.96 * se,
         CI_upper = BP_avg + 1.96 * se,
         BP_type = "DBP"
      )
   
   # Combine DBP and SBP
   BP_by <- bind_rows(SBP_by, DBP_by)
   
   # Plot  BP weighted means with CI across var groups
   Var_label = lookup [[var]]
   
   ggplot(
      BP_by, 
      aes(x = .data[[var]], y = BP_avg)
   ) +
      geom_point() +
      geom_errorbar(
         aes(
            ymin = CI_lower, 
            ymax = CI_upper
         ),
         width = 0.15
      ) +
      facet_wrap(
         ~BP_type, 
         scales = "free_y"
      ) +
      labs(
         title = paste0("Survey-weighted mean BP by ", Var_label, " (with 95% CI)"),
         x = Var_label,
         y = "Mean BP (mmHg)"
      ) +
      theme(
         axis.text.x = element_text(
            angle = 45,
            hjust = 1
         )
      )
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

plot_categorical("Race") +
      labs(title = "Figure 2: Differences in weighted mean BP with 95% CI across race/ethnici groups")
```

Marital status was significantly associated with SBP (overall p \<0.001). Compared with never-married participants, those who were married or living with a partner had a 3.12 mmHg lower SBP (95% CI: 1.32–4.91, p = 0.001), while widowed, divorced, or separated participants had a 7.52 mmHg lower SBP (95% CI: 5.42–9.62, p \<0.001). Married or cohabiting participants also had lower SBP than widowed, divorced, or separated participants (4.40 mmHg, 95% CI: 2.56–6.24, p \<0.001). For DBP, the overall association with marital status did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.069).

Education level was significantly associated with both SBP (p \<0.001) and DBP (p = 0.021). However, most Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons were not statistically significant. For SBP, the only statistically significant pairwise difference was between high school graduates/GED or equivalent and college graduates or above, with the former having higher SBP by approximately 4.62 mmHg (95% CI: 2.18–7.06, p \<0.001). For DBP, participants with some college or an associate degree had higher DBP than college graduates or above (1.92 mmHg, 95% CI: 0.35–3.50, p = 0.016). The remaining education-level comparisons were not statistically significant after Tukey adjustment.

Diabetes status was only significantly associated with SBP (p \<0.001) (see Figure 3). Participants with diabetes had a weighted mean SBP approximately 6.06 mmHg lower than participants without diabetes (95% CI: 3.70–8.42, p \<0.001). The differences involving borderline diabetes were not statistically significant.

Use of BP-lowering medication was significantly associated with SBP and DBP (both p \<0.001). Participants not taking BP-lowering medication had a higher weighted mean SBP compared to not diagnosed participants by 11.37 mmHg (95% CI: 6.98 - 15.77, p \<0.001). Meanwhile, participants taking BP-lowering medication had a higher weighted mean SBP compared to not diagnosed participants by 12.07 mmHg (95% CI: 10.36 - 13.77, p \<0.001). In contrast, participants not taking BP-lowering medication had a weighted mean DBP 3.87 mmHg higher than those taking BP-lowering medication and 7.01 mmHg higher than not diagnosed participants (p = 0.003, \<0.001, respectively). Participants taking BP-lowering medication had a higher weighted mean DBP compared to not diagnosed participants by 3.14 mmHg (p \<0.001).

Health insurance status was not significantly associated with either SBP or DBP (p = 0.138 and p = 0.877, respectively). All plots will be provided in the “descriptive plots” supplementary file.

#### 3.2.2 Relationship with continuous covariates

The correlation heat map of continuous variables demonstrates expected relationships between BP and continuous variables. The map shows a positive correlation between mean SBP and mean DBP (r = 0.63, p \<0.001). Mean SBP additionally showed a positive correlation with age (r = 0.39, p \<0.001) and a weaker positive correlation with both HbA1c (r = 0.18, p \<0.001) and log-transformation of ACR (r = 0.24, p \<0.001). In contrast, a negative association was observed between SBP and pulse rate (r = -0.04, p = 0.007) and with the log-transformation of eGFR (r = -0.25, p \<0.001). Mean DBP exhibited positive correlations with pulse rate (r = 0.28, p \<0.001), WC (r = 0.27, p \<0.001), BMI (r = 0.25, p \<0.001), HbA1c (r = 0.11, p \<0.001), and log ACR (r = 0.1, p \<0.001). Pulse rate was correlated with age, IPR, WC, BMI, HbA1c, log ACR, and log eGFR (r = -0.16, -0.11, 0.12, 0.13, 0.12, 0.08, 0.13, respectively; all p \<0.001).

The correlation heat map also illustrates clustering among the variables, including a negative correlation between log ACR and log eGFR (r = -0.21, p \<0.001). Age was positively correlated with IRP (r = 0.08, p \<0.001), HbA1c (r = 0.27, p \<0.001), and log ACR (r = 0.26, p \<0.001), while it was negatively correlated with log eGFR (r = -0.63, p \<0.001). Another clustering was among anthropometric measures; BMI was strongly correlated with WC (r = 0.90, p \<0.001). Figure 4 demonstrates the correlation heat map between the continuous covariates.

Overall, these findings were consistent with established physiological relationships and provided valuable information regarding potential multicollinearity among predictors before the development of multivariable regression.

```{r}
#| include: false

# ==== Correlation Map Heat ====

# 1. Calculate survey‐weighted Pearson correlation
cor_result <- svycor(
   ~ SBP_avg + DBP_avg + Pulse_avg + Age + IPR + WC + BMI + HbA1c + 
      ACR_log + eGFR_log,
   design = NHANES_design,
   sig.stats = TRUE,
   bootn = 2000
)

# 2. Extract correlation and p-value matrices
cor_matrix <- cor_result$cors
p_matrix <- cor_result$p.values

# 3. Fix labels
rownames(cor_matrix) <- lookup[rownames(cor_matrix)]
colnames(cor_matrix) <- lookup[colnames(cor_matrix)]

rownames(p_matrix) <- lookup[rownames(p_matrix)]
colnames(p_matrix) <- lookup[colnames(p_matrix)]

# 4. Convert correlation matrix to long format
cor_long <- as.data.frame(cor_matrix) %>%
   rownames_to_column("Variable1") %>%
   pivot_longer(
      -Variable1,
      names_to = "Variable2",
      values_to = "r"
   )

p_long <- as.data.frame(p_matrix) %>%
   rownames_to_column("Variable1") %>%
   pivot_longer(
      -Variable1,
      names_to = "Variable2",
      values_to = "p"
   )

# 5. Combine them and make star system
heatmap_data <- cor_long %>%
   left_join(
      p_long,
      by = c("Variable1", "Variable2")
   ) %>%
   mutate(
      Variable1 = factor(Variable1, levels = colnames(cor_matrix)),
      Variable2 = factor(Variable2, levels = rev(colnames(cor_matrix)))
   ) %>%
   filter(Variable1 != Variable2) %>%
   mutate(
      stars = case_when(
         p < 0.001 ~ "***",
         p < 0.01  ~ "**",
         p < 0.05  ~ "*",
         TRUE      ~ ""
      )
   )
```

### 3.3 Weighted multivariable regression models

Survey-weighted multivariable linear regression was used to estimate independent adjusted associations with SBP and DBP. The primary clinical specification differed between the two outcomes. For SBP, the primary model included WC, log-transformed ACR, and HbA1c. For DBP, the primary model included BMI, log-transformed eGFR, and HbA1c. Both models additionally included the prespecified demographic and socioeconomic variables. Heart rate was subsequently added to the primary model.

#### 3.3.1 Alternative specifications models

Eight alternative specifications were examined for each outcome by substituting alternative measures of adiposity (WC versus BMI), renal function (log-transformed ACR versus log-transformed eGFR), and glycemic status (HbA1c versus categorical diabetes status). Maximum VIF and model deviance were reported to characterize multicollinearity and model fit, respectively. For SBP, maximum VIF values ranged from 3.11 to 21.09, and deviance ranged from 952,219.3 to 976,742.7. Model 1 had a maximum VIF of 3.11 and a deviance of 953,323.6 and was chosen as the primary SBP model. For DBP, maximum VIF values ranged from 4.58 to 7.39, with deviance ranging from 448,614.4 to 455,620.7. Model 7 was chosen as the primary DBP model.

```{r}
#| include: false

# ==== Weighted multivariable regression ====

## ==== Create new design ====

# Copy design
MultiM_design <- NHANES_design

# New race variable with 3 groups 
MultiM_design$variables$Race_new <- factor(
   ifelse(
      MultiM_design$variables$Race == "Non Hispanic White",
      "Non Hispanic White",
      ifelse(
         MultiM_design$variables$Race == "Non Hispanic Black",
         "Non Hispanic Black",
         "Other Racial Groups"
      )
   ),
   levels = c("Non Hispanic White","Non Hispanic Black", "Other Racial Groups")
)

# New education variable with 2 groups
MultiM_design$variables$Education_new <- factor(
   ifelse(
      MultiM_design$variables$Education %in% c(
         "Less than 9th grade",
         "9-11th grade (Includes 12th grade with no diploma)"
      ),
      "12th grade or Less",
      "High school graduate/GED or above"
   ),
   levels = c("12th grade or Less", "High school graduate/GED or above")
)

## ==== Alternative model specifications ====
Alter_mod_tab <- function(BP){
   
   # Model formulas
   Mformulas <- list(
      
      M1 = paste0(
         BP, "_avg ~ Age + Sex + Race_new + Marital_status + Education_new +
         IPR + Insurance + WC + ACR_log + HbA1c"
      ),
      
      M2 = paste0(
         BP, "_avg ~ Age + Sex + Race_new + Marital_status + Education_new +
      IPR + Insurance + WC + ACR_log + Diabetes"
      ),
      
      M3 = paste0(
         BP, "_avg ~ Age + Sex + Race_new + Marital_status +
      Education_new + IPR + Insurance +
      WC + eGFR_log + HbA1c"
      ),
      
      M4 = paste0(
         BP, "_avg ~ Age + Sex + Race_new + Marital_status +
      Education_new + IPR + Insurance +
      WC + eGFR_log + Diabetes"
      ),
      
      M5 = paste0(
         BP, "_avg ~ Age + Sex + Race_new + Marital_status +
      Education_new + IPR + Insurance +
      BMI + ACR_log + HbA1c"
      ),
      
      M6 = paste0(
         BP, "_avg ~ Age + Sex + Race_new + Marital_status +
      Education_new + IPR + Insurance +
      BMI + ACR_log + Diabetes"
      ),
      
      M7 = paste0(
         BP, "_avg ~ Age + Sex + Race_new + Marital_status +
      Education_new + IPR + Insurance +
      BMI + eGFR_log + HbA1c"
      ),
      
      M8 = paste0(
         BP, "_avg ~ Age + Sex + Race_new + Marital_status +
      Education_new + IPR + Insurance +
      BMI + eGFR_log + Diabetes"
      )
   )
   
   # Fitting models
   Models <- map(
      Mformulas,
      \(f) svyglm(f, design = MultiM_design)
   )
   
   # VIFs
   vifs <- map(
      Models, 
      vif
   )
   
   # Deviance
   DV <- map(
      Models, 
      deviance
   )
   
   # Return results as a table
   table <- tibble(
      Model = c("Model 1", "Model 2", "Model 3", "Model 4", "Model 5", "Model 6", "Model 7", "Model 8"),
      
      Adiposity = c(rep(c("WC", "BMI"),  each = 4)),
      
      Renal = c(rep(c("ACR","eGFR"), times = 2, each = 2)),
      
      Glycemic = c(rep(c("HbA1c","Diabetes"), times = 4)),
      
      Max_VIF = map_dbl(
         vifs,
         \(x) max(x[, "GVIF^(1/(2*Df))"])
      ),
      
      Deviance = as.numeric(DV)
   )
   
   # Present it in a tidy way
   table %>% 
      gt()  %>%
      cols_align(
         align = "center",
         columns = c(
            Adiposity,
            Renal,
            Glycemic,
            Max_VIF,
            Deviance
         )
      ) %>%
      fmt_number(
         columns = Max_VIF,
         decimals = 2
      ) %>% 
      cols_label(
         Max_VIF = "Maximum VIF"
      ) %>%
      tab_footnote(
         footnote = "ACR and eGFR were log-transformed before analysis.",
         locations = cells_column_labels(columns = "Renal")
      )  %>%
      tab_footnote(
         footnote = "HbA1c was modeled as a continuous variable, whereas diabetes status was modeled as a categorical variable (yes, no, borderline).",
         locations = cells_column_labels(columns = "Glycemic")
      ) %>%
      tab_footnote(
         footnote = "Model adjusted for age (continuous), sex (male, female), race/ethnicity (Non-Hispanic White, Non-Hispanic Black, other racial groups), marital status (never married, married/living with partner, widowed/divorced/separated), education (< or ≥12th grade), IPR (continuous), and insurance status (yes/no) plus adiposity,	renal, and glycemic variables.",
         locations = cells_column_labels(columns = "Model")
      ) 
}

# Apply function on SBP outcome

## ==== Basic vs primary vs extended models ====
Coef_comp_tab <- function(BP, Adiposity, Renal){
   
   # Renal log variable
   Renal_log <- paste0(Renal, "_log")
   
   # Basic model

      "Age", "IPR"
   )

      reformulate(Basic_vars, response = paste0(BP, "_avg")),
      design = MultiM_design
   )
   
   # Primary model

      Basic_vars, Adiposity , Renal_log, "HbA1c"
   )
   
   Primary_Mod <- svyglm(
      reformulate(Primary_vars, response = paste0(BP, "_avg")),

   )
   
   # Extended model for pulse rate

      Primary_vars, "Pulse_avg"

   )
   
   # Format B (95% CI) + stars
   Format_coef <- function(model, variable) {
      
      Beta <- coef(model)[variable]

      Stars <- case_when(
         P < 0.001 ~ "***",
         P < 0.01  ~ "**",
         P < 0.05  ~ "*",
         TRUE      ~ ""
      )
      
      sprintf(
         "%.3f (%.3f - %.3f)%s",
         Beta,
         CI[1],
         CI[2],
         Stars
      )
   }

         # Education
         "", 
         "Ref",
         Format_coef(Basic_Mod, "Education_newHigh school graduate/GED or above"),
         
         # Insurance
         "", 
         "Ref",
         Format_coef(Basic_Mod, "InsuranceCovered"),
         
         # Age
         Format_coef(Basic_Mod, "Age"),
         
         # IPR
         Format_coef(Basic_Mod, "IPR"),
         
         # Adiposity
         "",
         
         # Renal
         "",
         
         # HbA1c
         "",
         
         # Pulse rate
         ""
      ),
      
      Primary = c(
         
         # Sex

         "Ref",
         Format_coef(Primary_Mod, "SexFemale"),

         # Education

         # HbA1c
         Format_coef(Primary_Mod, "HbA1c"),

         # IPR
         Format_coef(Pulse_Mod, "IPR"),
         
         # Adiposity

   # Return table in a tidy way
   table %>%
```

#### 3.3.2 SBP final model

In the fully adjusted model, female sex was associated with lower SBP compared with male sex (β = -6.10 mmHg, 95% CI: -8.73 to -3.47, p = 0.01). Compared with non-Hispanic White adults, non-Hispanic Black adults had higher SBP (β = 4.21 mmHg, 95% CI: 0.22 - 8.20, p = 0.045).

Age was positively associated with SBP (β = 0.35 mmHg per year, 95% CI: 0.25 - 0.45, p = 0.005). Higher log-transformed ACR was also associated with higher SBP (β = 4.70, 95% CI: 0.53 - 8.88, p = 0.040).

No statistically significant associations were observed for the rest covariates, including WC (β = 0.02 mmHg per unit, p = 0.291), HbA1c (β = 0.28, p = 0.521), mean pulse rate (β = 0.02 mmHg per beat/min, p = 0.521), IPR (p = 0.236), education (p = 0.969), insurance status (p = 0.986), marital status (p ≥ 0.142), or the other racial-group category (p = 0.501).

Heart rate was subsequently added to the primary model. In the resulting extended survey-weighted model, the maximum VIF was 4.42, and deviance was 953,004.3, representing a modest reduction in deviance relative to the primary model. However, it did not change the direction of the principal associations observed in the primary model. All coefficients remained broadly similar after its inclusion.

#### 3.3.3 DBP final model

The pattern of associations for DBP differed from that observed for SBP. In the extended DBP model, female sex was associated with lower DBP compared with male sex (β = -3.12 mmHg, 95% CI: -5.14 to -1.10, p = 0.22). Non-Hispanic Black adults had higher DBP than non-Hispanic White adults (β = 3.74 mmHg, 95% CI: 0.99 - 6.50, p = 0.028).

BMI was positively associated with DBP. Each one-unit increase in BMI was associated with a 0.31 mmHg higher DBP (95% CI: 0.19 - 0.44, p = 0.009). Mean pulse rate was also positively associated with DBP, with each additional beat per minute associated with a 0.26 mmHg higher DBP (95% CI: 0.18 - 0.33, p = 0.004).

Age was not statistically significantly associated with DBP after multivariable adjustment (β = 0.05, p = 0.104). Likewise, log-transformed eGFR (β = 2.98, p = 0.255) and HbA1c (β = 0.013, p = 0.971) were not significantly associated with DBP in the extended model. No statistically significant associations were observed for IRP (p = 0.408), education (p = 0.556), insurance status (p = 0.863), marital status (p ≥ 0.079), or the other racial-group category (p = 0.684).

The extended survey-weighted model had a maximum VIF equal to 6.22, and deviance was 419,204.3, representing a reduction in deviance relative to the primary model but maximum VIF was dramatically increased. The pulse rate addition also changed the magnitude of the principal associations observed in the primary model.

Overall, the adjusted associations differed between SBP and DBP. Age and log-transformed ACR were associated with SBP but not DBP, whereas BMI and pulse rate were associated with DBP but not SBP. The direction and significance of the sex and race/ethnicity associations were broadly consistent across both outcomes.

### 3.4 Prediction models

#### 3.4.1 Development and comparison of SBP and DBP predictive models

For SBP, ordinary linear regression achieved an RMSE of 15.525 mmHg, MAE of 11.747 mmHg, and R2 of 0.222 (Table 10). The penalized models produced very similar results. Ridge regression achieved an RMSE of 15.522 mmHg, MAE of 11.741 mmHg, and R2 of 0.223. Lasso regression achieved the lowest RMSE (15.516 mmHg) and MAE (11.734 mmHg), with an R2 of 0.223. Elastic Net regression, with a mixture parameter of 0.90 and penalty of 0.0954, had an RMSE of 15.516 mmHg, MAE of 11.735 mmHg, and R2 of 0.223. The final SBP model achieved a test-set RMSE of 15.284 mmHg, MAE of 11.621 mmHg, and R2 of 0.212 (Table 11).

For DBP, ordinary linear regression produced an RMSE of 9.928 mmHg, MAE of 7.657 mmHg, and R2 of 0.156. Ridge regression achieved the lowest RMSE (9.925 mmHg), with an MAE of 7.658 mmHg and R2 of 0.156. Lasso regression yielded an RMSE of 9.928 mmHg, MAE of 7.662 mmHg, and R2 of 0.155. Elastic Net regression, with a mixture parameter of 0.10 and penalty of 0.2442, achieved an RMSE of 9.927 mmHg, MAE of 7.661 mmHg, and R2 of 0.156. The final DBP model achieved a test-set RMSE of 9.673 mmHg, MAE of 7.602 mmHg, and R2 of 0.177.

```{r}
#| include: false

# ==== Prediction model ====

# Build a function to choose best model and select/investigate final model
BP_Model <- function(Outcome, BP_label) {
   
   ## ==== 1. Split data into train and test ====
   
   set.seed(1234)
   
   Split <- initial_split(
      Data, 
      prop = 0.8, 
      strata = !!sym(Outcome)
   )
   
   Train <- training(Split)
   Test  <- testing (Split)
   
   ## ==== 2. Create a recipe ====
   
   # Define variables
   
   Variables <- c( 
      "Age", "Sex", "Race", "Marital_status", "Education", "IPR", "Insurance", 
      "BMI", "WC", "ACR_log", "eGFR_log", "Diabetes", "HbA1c", "Taking_BP_meds",
      "Pulse_avg"
   )
   
   # Create a formula 
   BP_formula <- reformulate(
      termlabels = Variables,
      response = Outcome
   )
   
   # Create a recipe
   BP_recipe <- recipe(
      BP_formula,
      data = Train
   ) %>%
      step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%                 # Removes zero-variance predictors
      step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%      # Convert categorical predictors into dummy 
      step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())      # Standardize every numeric predictor
   
   ## ==== 3. Create 10-fold cross-validation ====
   Folds <- vfold_cv(
      Train,
      v = 10,
      repeats = 5,
      strata = !!sym(Outcome)
   )
   
   ## ==== 4. Create models ====
   
   ## Ordinary linear regression
   LM_spec <- linear_reg() %>%
      set_engine("lm")
   
   ## Penalized regression
   P_model <- linear_reg (
      penalty = tune(), 
      mixture = tune()
   ) %>%
      set_engine (engine = "glmnet") 
   
   ## ==== 5. Create workflows ====
   
   # Ordinary linear regression
   LM_WF <- workflow() %>%
      add_recipe(BP_recipe) %>%
      add_model(LM_spec)
   
   # Penalized regression
   P_WF <- workflow() %>% 
      add_recipe (BP_recipe) %>% 
      add_model(P_model)
   
   ## ==== 6. Create tuning grid ====
   Penalty_grid <- grid_regular(
      penalty(),
      mixture(range = c(0, 1)),  # Contains Ridge and Lasso regressions
      levels = c(50, 11)
   )
   
   ## ==== 7. Fit models ====
   
   # Ordinary linear regression
   LM_results <- fit_resamples(
      LM_WF,
      resamples = Folds,
      metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq),
      control = control_resamples(
         save_pred = TRUE
      )
   )
   
   # Penalized regression
   P_results <- tune_grid (
      P_WF, 
      resamples = Folds, 
      grid = Penalty_grid,
      metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq),
      control = control_grid(
         save_pred = TRUE
      )
   )
   
   ## ==== 8. Collect model results ====
   
   # Ordinary linear regression
   Best_LM <- collect_metrics(LM_results) 
   
   # Penalized regression
   P_metrics <- collect_metrics(P_results)
   
   ## ==== 9. Choose best penalty for each model ====
   
   # Ridge model
   Best_Ridge <- P_metrics %>%
      filter(
         .metric == "rmse",
         mixture == 0
      ) %>%
      slice_min(
         order_by = mean,
         n = 1,
         with_ties = FALSE
      )
   
   # Lasso model
   Best_Lasso <- P_metrics %>%
      filter(
         .metric == "rmse",
         mixture == 1
      ) %>%
      slice_min(
         order_by = mean,
         n = 1,
         with_ties = FALSE
      )
   
   # Elastic Net model
   Best_El <- P_metrics %>%
      filter(
         .metric == "rmse",
         mixture > 0,
         mixture < 1
      ) %>%
      slice_min(
         order_by = mean,
         n = 1,
         with_ties = FALSE
      )
   
   ## ==== 10. Create comparison table ====
   
   ## Ordinary linear regression
   LM_summary <- Best_LM %>%
      select(.metric, mean, std_err) %>%
      mutate(
         Model = "Ordinary linear regression",
         Mixture = NA_real_,
         Penalty = NA_real_
      )
   
   ## Ridge model
   Ridge_summary <- P_metrics %>%
      filter(.config == Best_Ridge$.config) %>%
      select(.metric, mean, std_err) %>%
      mutate(
         Model = "Ridge",
         Mixture = 0,
         Penalty = Best_Ridge$penalty
      )
   
   ## Lasso model
   Lasso_summary <- P_metrics %>%
      filter(.config == Best_Lasso$.config) %>%
      select(.metric, mean, std_err) %>%
      mutate(
         Model = "Lasso",
         Mixture = 1,
         Penalty = Best_Lasso$penalty
      )
   
   ## Elastic Net model
   El_summary <- P_metrics %>%
      filter(.config == Best_El$.config) %>%
      select(.metric, mean, std_err) %>%
      mutate(
         Model = "Elastic Net",
         Mixture = Best_El$mixture,
         Penalty = Best_El$penalty
      )
   
   ## Combine results in a tidy table
   Train_table <- bind_rows(
      LM_summary,
      Ridge_summary,
      Lasso_summary,
      El_summary
   ) %>%
      pivot_wider(
         names_from = .metric,
         values_from = c(mean, std_err)
      ) %>%
      mutate(
         Outcome = BP_label,
         Mixture = ifelse(
            is.na(Mixture),
            "—",
            sprintf("%.2f", Mixture)
         ),
         Penalty = ifelse(
            is.na(Penalty),
            "—",
            sprintf("%.4f", Penalty)
         ),
         RMSE = sprintf("%.4f", mean_rmse),
         MAE  = sprintf("%.4f", mean_mae),
         R2   = sprintf("%.4f", mean_rsq)
      ) %>%
      select(
         Outcome,
         Model,
         Mixture,
         Penalty,
         RMSE,
         MAE,
         R2
      )
   
   ## ==== 11. Select overall best penalized model ====
   
   Best_GLMNET <- select_best(
      P_results,
      metric = "rmse"
   )
   
   ## ==== 12. Tuning plot ====
   
   Tuning_RMSE <- P_metrics %>%
      filter(.metric == "rmse")
   
   Tuning_plot <- ggplot(
      Tuning_RMSE,
      aes(
         x = penalty,
         y = mean,
         group = factor(mixture),
         color = factor(mixture)
      )
   ) +
      geom_line() +
      geom_point(size = 1.3) +
      geom_point(
         data = Tuning_RMSE %>%
            filter(
               mixture == Best_GLMNET$mixture,
               penalty == Best_GLMNET$penalty
            ),
         aes(x = penalty, y = mean),
         size = 4,
         inherit.aes = FALSE
      ) +
      scale_x_log10() +
      labs(
         x = "Penalty (log scale)",
         y = "Mean cross-validated RMSE",
         color = "Lasso proportion",
         title = paste0("Hyperparameter tuning of", BP_label, "penalized regression models")
      ) 
   
   ## ==== 13. Select the final predictive model ====
   Final_WF <- finalize_workflow(
      P_WF, 
      Best_GLMNET
   )
   
   ## ==== 14. Fit the final predictive model ====
   Final_fit <- last_fit(
      Final_WF,
      split = Split,
      metrics = metric_set(
         rmse, 
         mae, 
         rsq
      )
   )
   
   # Final test performance
   Final_test_metrics <- collect_metrics(Final_fit) %>%
      pivot_wider(
         names_from = .metric,
         values_from = .estimate
      ) %>%
      mutate(
         Outcome = BP_label
      ) %>%
      select(
         Outcome,
         rmse,
         mae,
         rsq
      )
   
   Final_workflow <- extract_workflow(Final_fit)
   
   ## ==== 15. Extract coefficients from the final predictive model ====
   
   # Extract coefficients
   Final_coefficients <- Final_fit %>%
      extract_fit_parsnip() %>%
      tidy()
   
   Coefficient_table <- tibble(
      Variable = c(
         "Sex",
         "Male",
         "Female",
         
         "Race/ethnicity",
         "Mexican American",
         "Non Hispanic White",
         "Non Hispanic Black",
         "Non Hispanic Asian",
         "Other Hispanic",
         "Other Race",
         
         "Marital status",
         "Never married",
         "Married/Living with partner",
         "Widowed/Divorced/Separated",
         
         "Education",
         "Less than 9th grade",
         "9–11th grade (includes 12th grade with no diploma)",
         "High school graduate/GED or equivalent",
         "Some college or AA degree",
         "College graduate or above",
         
         "Insurance",
         "Not covered",
         "Covered",
         
         "Age",
         "IPR",
         "BMI",
         "WC",
         "eGFR",
         "ACR",
         "Mean Pulse rate",
         "HbA1c",
         
         "Diabetes",
         "No",
         "Yes",
         "Borderline",
         
         "BP-lowering medications",
         "Not diagnosed",
         "Not taking",
         "Taking"
      ),
      Estimate = c(
         NA,
         0,
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "Sex_Female"],
         
         NA,
         0,
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "Race_Non.Hispanic.White"],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "Race_Non.Hispanic.Black"],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "Race_Non.Hispanic.Asian"],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "Race_Other.Hispanic"],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "Race_Other.Race"],
         
         NA,
         0,
         Final_coefficients$estimate[
            Final_coefficients$term == "Marital_status_Married.Living.with.partner"
         ],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[
            Final_coefficients$term == "Marital_status_Widowed.Divorced.Separated"
         ],
         
         NA,
         0,
         Final_coefficients$estimate[
            Final_coefficients$term ==
               "Education_X9.11th.grade..Includes.12th.grade.with.no.diploma."
         ],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[
            Final_coefficients$term ==
               "Education_High.school.graduate.GED.or.equivalent"
         ],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[
            Final_coefficients$term ==
               "Education_Some.college.or.AA.degree"
         ],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[
            Final_coefficients$term ==
               "Education_College.graduate.or.above"
         ],
         
         NA,
         0,
         Final_coefficients$estimate[
            Final_coefficients$term == "Insurance_Covered"
         ],
         
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "Age"],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "IPR"],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "BMI"],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "WC"],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "eGFR_log"],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "ACR_log"],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "Pulse_avg"],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[Final_coefficients$term == "HbA1c"],
         
         NA,
         0,
         Final_coefficients$estimate[
            Final_coefficients$term == "Diabetes_Yes"
         ],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[
            Final_coefficients$term == "Diabetes_Borderline"
         ],
         
         NA,
         0,
         Final_coefficients$estimate[
            Final_coefficients$term == "Taking_BP_meds_Not.taking"
         ],
         Final_coefficients$estimate[
            Final_coefficients$term == "Taking_BP_meds_Taking"
         ]
      )
   ) %>%
      mutate(
         Estimate = round(Estimate, 3)
      ) %>% 
      gt() %>%
      text_transform(
         locations = cells_body(
            columns = Estimate,
            rows = Variable %in% c("Sex", "Race/ethnicity", "Marital status", "Education", "Insurance", "Diabetes", "BP-lowering medications")
         ),

            ""
         }

      text_transform(
         locations = cells_body(
```
