   # Final model diagnostic data
   Final_train_predictions <- predict(
      Final_workflow,
      new_data = Train
   ) %>%
      bind_cols(
         Train %>% select(all_of(Outcome))
      ) %>%
      rename(
         Observed = all_of(Outcome),
         Predicted = .pred
      ) %>%
      mutate(
         Residual = Observed - Predicted,
         Standardized_Residual = Residual / sd(Residual, na.rm = TRUE)
      ) 
   
   ## ==== 16. Diagnostic plots ====
   
   ### ==== Plot 1: Residuals vs fitted values ====
   
   Diagnostic_residuals <- ggplot(
      Final_train_predictions,
      aes(
         Predicted, 
         Residual)
   )  +
      geom_point(
         color = "#ff9800",
         alpha = 0.35
      ) +
      geom_smooth(
         method = "loess",
         se = TRUE
      ) +
      geom_hline(
         yintercept = 0,
         linetype = "dashed"
      ) +
      labs(
         x = "Fitted values (mmHg)",
         y = "Residuals (mmHg)",
         title = "Residuals versus fitted values"
      )
   
   ### ==== Plot 2: Normal Q-Q plot ====
   
   Diagnostic_QQ <- ggplot(
      Final_train_predictions,
      aes(
         sample = Residual
      )
   ) +
      stat_qq() +
      stat_qq_line() +
      labs(
         x = "Theoretical quantiles",
         y = "Standardized residuals",
         title = "Q-Q plot"
      )
   
   ### ==== Plot 3: Scale-location plot ====
   
   Diagnostic_scale <- ggplot(
      Final_train_predictions,
      aes(
         x = Predicted,
         y = sqrt(abs(Standardized_Residual))
      )
   ) +
      geom_point(
         color = "orange",
         alpha = 0.35
      ) +
      geom_smooth(
         method = "loess",
         se = TRUE
      ) +
      labs(
         x = "Fitted values (mmHg)",
         y = expression(sqrt("|Standardized residuals|")),
         title = "Scale-location"
      )
   
   ### ==== Plot 4: Residual histogram ====
   
   Diagnostic_residual_histogram <- ggplot(
      Final_train_predictions,
      aes(x = Residual)
   ) +
      geom_histogram(
         aes(y = after_stat(density)),
         bins = 30
      ) +
      geom_density() +
      geom_vline(
         xintercept = 0,
         linetype = "dashed"
      ) +
      labs(
         x = "Residual",
         y = "Density",
         title = "Residual Distribution"
      ) 
   
   ### ==== Combine four diagnostic plots ====
   
   Diagnostic_plots <- (
      Diagnostic_residuals +
         Diagnostic_QQ +
         Diagnostic_scale +
         Diagnostic_residual_histogram
   ) 
   
   ## ==== 17. Get results of train and test data ====
   
   # Cross-validation predictions
   CV_predictions <- collect_predictions(P_results) %>%
      filter(
         .config == Best_GLMNET$.config
      )
   
   CV_predictions_mean <- CV_predictions %>%
      group_by(.row) %>%
      summarise(
         Observed = first(.data[[Outcome]]),
         Predicted = mean(.pred, na.rm = TRUE),
         .groups = "drop"
      ) %>%
      mutate(
         Residual = Observed - Predicted,
         Dataset = "Cross-validation"
      )
   
   # Held-out test results
   Test_predictions <- Test %>%
      bind_cols(
         predict(
            Final_workflow,
            new_data = Test
         )
      ) %>%
      rename(
         Observed = .data[[Outcome]],
         Predicted = .pred,
      ) %>%
      mutate(
         Residual = Observed - Predicted,
         Dataset = "Held-out test"
      )
   
   # Combine test and train data
   Prediction_plot_data <- bind_rows(
      CV_predictions_mean,
      Test_predictions
   )
   
   ## ==== 18. Observed vs predicted plot for CV ====
   
   Prediction_plot <- ggplot(
      Prediction_plot_data,
      aes(
         x = Observed,
         y = Predicted
      )
   ) +
      geom_point(
         color = "orange",
         alpha = 0.35
      ) +
      geom_abline(
         slope = 1,
         intercept = 0,
         linetype = "dashed"
      ) +
      facet_wrap(
         ~ Dataset,
         ncol = 2
      ) +
      coord_equal() +
      labs(
         x = paste("Observed", BP_label, "(mmHg)"),
         y = paste("Predicted", BP_label, "(mmHg)"),
         title = paste(
            "Observed versus predicted",
            BP_label
         ),
         subtitle = "Cross-validated predictions versus held-out test predictions"
      )
   
   ## ==== 19. Categorical subgroup performance ====
   
   # Create a function to return a table with RMSE, MAE, R2, and mean error
   Cate_Subgroup_table <- function(vars){
      
      # Create an empty table
      tab <- tibble()
      
      # Create a function to calculate RMSE, MAE, R2, and mean error
      Categorical_metrics <- function(data) {
         
         data %>%
            summarise(
               RMSE = sqrt(
                  mean(Residual^2, na.rm = TRUE)
               ),
               
               MAE = mean(
                  abs(Residual),
                  na.rm = TRUE
               ),
               
               Mean_Error = mean(
                  Residual,
                  na.rm = TRUE
               ),
               
               R2 = 1 -
                  sum(
                     Residual^2,
                     na.rm = TRUE
                  ) /
                  sum(
                     (
                        Observed - mean(Observed, na.rm = TRUE)
                     )^2,
                     na.rm = TRUE
                  ),
               n = n()
            )
      }
      
      # Apply function for each variable 
      for(var in vars){
         
         result <- Test_predictions %>%
            group_by(
               Group = .data[[var]]
            ) %>%
            Categorical_metrics() %>%
            ungroup() %>%
            mutate(
               Variable = lookup[[var]],
               .before = Group
            )
         
         tab <- bind_rows(
            tab,
            result
         )
      }
      
      # Format final table
      tab <- tab %>%
         mutate(
            RMSE = sprintf("%.3f", RMSE),
            MAE = sprintf("%.3f", MAE),
            Mean_Error = sprintf("%.3f", Mean_Error),
            R2 = sprintf("%.3f", R2)
         ) %>%
         select(
            Variable,
            Group,
            n,
            RMSE,
            MAE,
            Mean_Error,
            R2
         )
      
      # Return results
      tab
   }
   
   # Apply function on categorical variables
   Cat_sub_tab <- Cate_Subgroup_table(
      c(
         "Sex", "Race", "Taking_BP_meds", "Diabetes"
      )
   ) 
   
   ## ==== 20. Residual analysis for continuous variables ====
   
   Plot_residual <- function(vars) {
      
      # Apply function for each variable
      map (
         vars, 
         function(var) {
            
            ggplot(
               Test_predictions,
               aes(
                  x = .data[[var]],
                  y = Residual
               )
            ) +
               geom_point(
                  color = "orange",
                  alpha = 0.35
               ) +
               geom_smooth(
                  method = "loess",
                  se = TRUE
               ) +
               geom_hline(
                  yintercept = 0,
                  linetype = "dashed"
               ) +
               labs(
                  x = lookup[[var]],
                  y = "Prediction residual (mmHg)"
               )
         }
      )
   }
   
   # Apply function on continuous variables
   Residual_plots <- wrap_plots(
      Plot_residual(
         c(
            "Age", "BMI", "WC", "ACR_log", "eGFR_log", "HbA1c", "Pulse_avg"
         )
      ),
      ncol = 3
   ) 
   
   ## ====21. Function returns ====
   list(
      Best_LM = Best_LM,
      Best_Ridge = Best_Ridge,
      Best_Lasso = Best_Lasso,
      Best_El = Best_El,
      Best_GLMNET = Best_GLMNET,
      
      Train_table = Train_table,
      Tuning_plot = Tuning_plot,
      
      Final_WF = Final_WF,
      Final_test_metrics = Final_test_metrics,
      
      Coefficient_table = Coefficient_table,
      Prediction_plot = Prediction_plot,
      Diagnostic_plots = Diagnostic_plots,
      
      Cat_sub_tab = Cat_sub_tab,
      Residual_plots = Residual_plots
   )
}

The differences in predictive performance between the candidate models were negligible for both outcomes. The improvement in RMSE compared with ordinary linear regression was approximately 0.009 mmHg for SBP and 0.003 mmHg for DBP. These differences indicate that regularization provided little practical improvement in predictive accuracy for either outcome using the current predictor set. However, lasso model was selected as a final model for SBP, while ridge was selected for DBP. The cross-validation results also showed that the SBP model explained a larger proportion of outcome variability than the DBP model, with R2 values of approximately 0.223 and 0.156, respectively.

#### 3.4.2 Predictive model coefficients

For SBP, the largest positive continuous-predictor coefficients were observed for age (5.076) and log-transformed ACR (2.931) (refer to Table 12). Positive coefficients were also observed for HbA1c (0.867) and log-transformed eGFR (0.743). Negative coefficients were observed for female sex (−2.101), diabetes status classified as yes (−1.503), BMI (−0.175), WC (−0.056), and mean pulse rate (−0.394). The coefficient for non-Hispanic Black participants was positive (1.239), while several other race/ethnicity and education coefficients were shrunk to zero. The BP-lowering medication categories had positive coefficients of 2.554 for participants classified as not taking medication and 2.562 for those taking medication, relative to the reference category of not diagnosed.

```{r}
#| echo: false

SBP_Model$Coefficient_table
```

For DBP, female sex had a coefficient of −0.755 relative to males, while the coefficient for non-Hispanic Black participants was 1.138 relative to Mexican American participants (Table 13). Diabetes status classified as yes had a coefficient of −1.696, and the coefficient for participants taking BP-lowering medication was 0.395 relative to those classified as not diagnosed. Mean pulse rate had a positive coefficient of 2.720. Positive coefficients were also observed for WC (1.152), BMI (0.811), log-transformed ACR (0.826), log-transformed eGFR (0.572), HbA1c (0.399), age (0.245), and IPR (0.413).

```{r}
#| echo: false

DBP_Model$Coefficient_table
```

#### 3.4.3 Predictive performance across demographic and clinical subgroups

Subgroup analyses of the held-out test predictions showed that prediction error varied across sex, race/ethnicity, BP-lowering medication status, and diabetes status, see Table 14 and Table 15. The SBP subgroup results included 879 participants, whereas the DBP subgroup results included 878 participants.

```{r}
#| echo: false

DBP_Model$Cat_sub_tab

```

**Sex**

For SBP, prediction performance was similar between males and females in absolute error terms. Males had an RMSE of 15.116 mmHg and MAE of 11.386 mmHg, while females had an RMSE of 15.426 mmHg and MAE of 11.821 mmHg. The corresponding R2 values were 0.068 and 0.286.

For DBP, females had lower prediction errors than males. The RMSE was 9.302 mmHg among females and 10.116 mmHg among males; MAE was 7.384 and 7.873 mmHg, respectively. Their R2 values were 0.176 and 0.172.

Thus, absolute prediction errors were similar between the sexes for both outcomes, although the amount of explained variation differed across sex-specific groups.

**Race and ethnicity**

For SBP, RMSE ranged from 12.660 mmHg among Mexican American participants to 18.284 mmHg among non-Hispanic Black participants. Other Race participants also had relatively high prediction error, with an RMSE of 17.638 mmHg. The corresponding R2 values ranged from 0.167 among non-Hispanic Black participants to 0.301 among Other Hispanic participants.

For DBP, RMSE ranged from 9.193 mmHg among non-Hispanic White participants to 11.377 mmHg among Other Race participants. Non-Hispanic Asian participants had an RMSE of 10.930 mmHg, while non-Hispanic Black participants had an RMSE of 10.575 mmHg. The R2 values ranged from 0.129 among Other Race participants to 0.230 among non-Hispanic Asian participants.

These findings indicate that prediction error was not uniform across racial and ethnic subgroups. However, subgroup sample sizes differed substantially, ranging from 47 to 576 participants for SBP and 51 to 553 for DBP. Estimates for smaller groups should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

**BP-lowering medication status**

Medication status was associated with notable differences in prediction accuracy for both outcomes. For SBP, participants classified as not diagnosed had the lowest RMSE (13.225 mmHg), compared with 17.882 mmHg among participants not taking BP-lowering medication and 18.881 mmHg among those taking medication. MAE followed the same pattern, at 10.237, 12.620, and 14.726 mmHg, respectively. The R2 was particularly low among participants taking medication (0.043).

For DBP, participants classified as not diagnosed again had the lowest RMSE (8.475 mmHg), whereas participants not taking medication had an RMSE of 10.343 mmHg, and those taking medication had an RMSE of 11.682 mmHg. MAE ranged from 6.749 mmHg among those classified as not diagnosed to 9.339 mmHg among those taking medication. The R2 values were 0.145, 0.205, and 0.151, respectively.

Taken together, the results indicate that prediction errors were larger among participants taking BP-lowering medication than among those classified as not diagnosed, for both SBP and DBP. However, the R2 values did not follow exactly the same pattern as RMSE, illustrating the difference between absolute prediction error and the proportion of within-group variability explained by the model.

**Diabetes status**

For SBP, the RMSE was 14.911 mmHg among participants without diabetes, 17.425 mmHg among participants with diabetes, and 15.962 mmHg among those with borderline diabetes. The corresponding R2 values were 0.232, 0.087, and 0.044.

For DBP, the RMSE was 9.412 mmHg among participants without diabetes and 11.117 mmHg among those with diabetes. Participants with borderline diabetes had an RMSE of 8.898 mmHg. The R2 values were 0.166, 0.168, and 0.331, respectively.

Participants with diabetes therefore had higher absolute prediction errors than participants without diabetes for both outcomes. The apparently higher R2 among participants with borderline diabetes in the DBP model should be interpreted cautiously because that subgroup included only 30 participants. As with the other subgroups, R2 depends on the variability of the outcome within each group and does not directly measure the size of prediction errors.

**Mean prediction error**

Mean prediction error, defined as observed minus predicted BP, was generally small relative to the RMSE for both outcomes. Positive values indicate underprediction, whereas negative values indicate overprediction.

For SBP, subgroup mean errors ranged from −2.127 mmHg among Mexican American participants to +1.628 mmHg among non-Hispanic Asian participants. Mean error was −0.328 mmHg among participants taking BP-lowering medication and +0.095 mmHg among participants with diabetes.

For DBP, mean errors were also relatively small in most subgroups. The largest absolute subgroup mean errors were observed among participants not taking BP-lowering medication (−1.748 mmHg), Other Race participants (−1.629 mmHg), and Other Hispanic participants (−1.477 mmHg). These values suggest that average bias was relatively modest overall, even though individual-level errors—as reflected by RMSE and MAE—remained substantial.

#### 3.4.4 Diagnostic assessment of both predictive models

The diagnostic plots showed several common features in the SBP and DBP models (see Figures 5 and 6). For both outcomes, residuals were generally centered around zero across much of the fitted-value range. However, the residual-versus-fitted and scale-location plots suggested that residual variance was not entirely constant. In particular, the scale-location plots showed increasing residual spread toward higher fitted values, suggesting less consistent prediction errors in this region.

```{r}
#| echo: false

SBP_Model$Diagnostic_plots +
   plot_annotation(
      title = "Figure 5: Diagnostic plots for final SBP predictive model"
   )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

DBP_Model$Diagnostic_plots +
   plot_annotation(
      title = "Figure 6: Diagnostic plots for final DBP predictive model"
   )
```

The normal Q-Q plots showed reasonable alignment with the reference line near the center of the residual distribution, with noticeable deviations in the tails. The residual distributions were broadly uni-modal but showed some asymmetry and tail departures from normality.

Observed-versus-predicted plots suggested that the models tended to compress predicted values toward the middle of the observed distributions, refer to Figures 7 and 8. Consequently, the models had difficulty predicting individuals with unusually high or low BP values. This pattern was consistent with regression toward the mean.

```{r}
#| echo: false

SBP_Model$Prediction_plot +
   labs(
      title = "Figure 7: Observed versus predicted final SBP model"
   )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

DBP_Model$Prediction_plot +
   labs(
      title = "Figure 8: Observed versus predicted final DBP model"
   )
```

Examination of residual plots against continuous predictors suggested generally limited systematic residual patterns across the central ranges of most predictors. For SBP, see Figure 9, residual smooths were largely flat across age and log-transformed ACR, while some curvature or directional trends were apparent at higher values of BMI, waist circumference, HbA1c, and pulse rate. For DBP, a curved pattern was most apparent across age, with additional potential residual structure across BMI, log-transformed eGFR, and HbA1c (Figure 10). These patterns were less certain at the extremes of the predictor distributions, where observations were sparse, and confidence bands widened.

```{r}
#| echo: false

SBP_Model$Residual_plots +
      plot_annotation(
         title = " Figure 9: Prediction error across continuous variables in SBP final prediction model"
         ) +
   plot_layout(
      axes = "collect_y",
      axis_titles = "collect_y"
   ) 
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

DBP_Model$Residual_plots +
      plot_annotation(
         title = " Figure 10: Prediction error across continuous variables in DBP final prediction model"
         ) +
   plot_layout(
      axes = "collect_y",
      axis_titles = "collect_y"
   ) 
```

Taken together, the diagnostics suggest that both models captured broad relationships in the data but left some systematic variation unexplained.

## 4.0 Discussion

### 4.1 Adjusted associations with blood pressure

The observed racial and ethnic differences in BP were broadly consistent with previous US population-based research [13-15]. In unadjusted comparisons, non-Hispanic Black adults had higher BP than several other racial and ethnic groups, whereas in adjusted final models, they had higher adjusted SBP and DBP than non-Hispanic White adults. These differences should not be interpreted as direct biological effects of race or ethnicity, but considered in the context of socioeconomic conditions, health-related behaviors, healthcare access, environmental exposures, comorbidities, and structural factors [16-18]. Female sex was associated with lower SBP and DBP after adjustment, although the cross-sectional design does not establish the mechanisms underlying these differences. The socioeconomic associations were less consistent across the sequential models: associations involving IPR and marital status were attenuated after additional clinical covariates were included, while education and insurance coverage were not significantly associated with either outcome across the models. These results indicate that the estimated associations were sensitive to model specification; they do not demonstrate that clinical characteristics mediated socioeconomic associations or that socioeconomic circumstances are unimportant to cardiovascular health [19, 20]. Age was positively associated with SBP in both the basic and fully adjusted model, whereas no statistically significant adjusted association was observed with DBP. This pattern is broadly consistent with evidence that SBP tends to increase with age, whereas DBP may plateau or decline in later adulthood, partly in association with increasing arterial stiffness [21]. Nevertheless, because NHANES provides cross-sectional data, these findings describe differences between individuals of different ages rather than within-person changes over time.

The association of adiposity differed by BP component. In the extended model, WC was not significantly associated with SBP, whereas BMI was associated with DBP. This component-specific pattern should be interpreted in the context of evidence linking both general and central adiposity to hypertension risk [22]. However, this evidence is not directly equivalent to the present results, since this study looks at adjusted associations with continuous values of SBP and DBP rather than the incidence of hypertension. BMI and WC were strongly correlated in this analysis, and alternative model specifications indicated that the choice of adiposity measure influenced the model estimates and multicollinearity. These findings highlight the need to evaluate BMI and WC as alternative, correlated measures of adiposity rather than assuming that their individual coefficients reflect distinct effects [22].

Renal characteristics also showed outcome-specific patterns. Higher log-transformed ACR was associated with higher SBP, consistent with evidence linking albuminuria to elevated BP and vascular abnormalities [23, 24]. Whereas log-transformed eGFR was insignificantly associated with DBP, however, this finding does not establish the absence of an association, which may depend on the distribution of kidney function, model specification, and adjustment for correlated characteristics. ACR and eGFR provide complementary information about kidney health and should not be considered interchangeable measures [25, 26].

The alternative model specifications that used categorical diabetes status differed from those that used continuous HbA1c in their multicollinearity diagnostics and other model characteristics. Continuous HbA1c and categorical diabetes status reflect different aspects of glycemic health and may yield different associations with BP [27]. In the extended models, however, HbA1c was not significantly associated with either SBP or DBP after adjustment for the other measured covariates. This does not prove that glycemic status has no relationship with BP; instead, the models provided insufficient evidence of an adjusted association.

In the extended model, pulse rate was not found to be significantly associated with SBP but it was positively associated with DBP. This pattern differs partly from the findings of the WHO-CARDIAC study, which reported positive associations of resting heart rate with both BP components [28]. Additionally, there are studies have linked higher resting heart rate to the development of hypertension [29]; however, that evidence is not directly equivalent to a cross-sectional association with continuous BP components. Differences in study populations, covariate adjustment, and analytical design may contribute to the variation in findings. Furthermore, the difference in statistical significance between SBP and DBP does not, by itself, establish that their associations with pulse rate differ significantly.

Current antihypertensive medication use was not included in the primary adjusted models because treatment status may reflect prior hypertension and related clinical factors. Consequently, the primary estimates describe associations with measured BP without conditioning on current medication use. Unadjusted comparisons involving medication use should not be interpreted as estimates of treatment effectiveness because of potential confounding by indication.

### 4.2 Prediction performance

The predictive models showed modest performance. The SBP model achieved a cross-validation RMSE of 15.52 mmHg and R² of 0.223, compared with 9.93 mmHg and 0.156 for DBP, respectively. The held-out test-set results were broadly consistent with the cross-validation findings, although the models explained only a limited proportion of individual-level variation. The higher R² for SBP indicates that the model explained a greater proportion of its observed variance than the DBP model, despite the higher absolute prediction error for SBP [30, 31]. This difference highlights the importance of interpreting RMSE and R² together because they represent different aspects of predictive performance [32].

Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net regressions provided slight improvements over ordinary linear regression, reducing RMSE by approximately 0.009 mmHg for SBP and 0.003 mmHg for DBP. Although regularization can reduce overfitting and address correlated predictors, its benefits depend on the data and model structure [31, 33]. In this analysis, changing the penalty structure alone did not materially improve predictive performance. The prediction coefficients should also not be interpreted as independent population-level associations or causal effects because correlated predictors may share predictive information and penalization can shrink or eliminate coefficients [34].

Prediction errors varied across subgroups. Non-Hispanic Black participants had the highest SBP RMSE, whereas participants in the Other Race category had the highest DBP RMSE. Participants taking BP-lowering medication and those with diabetes had higher RMSE for both SBP and DBP than their respective comparison groups. These findings identify subgroups warranting further evaluation but do not, by themselves, establish systematic model bias. Differences in subgroup sample size and outcome variability may affect the reliability and interpretation of performance metrics [30, 35].

Residual diagnostics also suggested that the linear models did not fully capture every relationship between the predictors and the outcome. Curvature was apparent for selected metabolic and anthropometric predictors. The observed-versus-predicted plots further suggested underprediction at higher BP values and overprediction at lower values, indicating reduced accuracy toward the extremes of the observed distribution [36, 37]. These patterns provide potential directions for model refinement. Future analyses could evaluate restricted cubic splines and a limited number of clinically justified interactions within the validation process. However, departures from residual normality alone are less informative about predictive performance than out-of-sample errors and systematic prediction patterns.

## 5.0 Conclusion

This study identified adjusted associations between selected demographic, anthropometric, metabolic, and renal characteristics and systolic and diastolic blood pressure among US adults using NHANES 2021–2023 data. The observed associations differed between SBP and DBP, underscoring the value of evaluating the two outcomes separately. Predictive performance was modest, with test-set R² values of 0.212 for SBP and 0.177 for DBP. Regularization provided negligible improvement over ordinary linear regression, indicating that it did not substantially improve prediction with the selected predictors and model specifications. Although the models captured some variation in BP, their predictive accuracy was limited at the individual level. In general, the findings distinguish the identification of population-level associations from the prediction of individual blood pressure values. The cross-sectional design also means that the observed associations should not be interpreted as causal effects.

## 6.0 Strengths, limitations, and future directions

A key strength of this study was the complementary use of survey-weighted regression and predictive modeling to address distinct research objectives. The survey-weighted analyses accounted for the complex NHANES sampling design when estimating adjusted associations, while the predictive analyses compared multiple regression approaches using repeated cross-validation and a held-out test set. Subgroup performance assessments and residual diagnostics provided additional insight into the limitations of prediction beyond overall performance metrics. Together, these approaches offered a broader assessment of the relationships between routinely available characteristics and BP, while distinguishing population-level associations from individual-level predictive performance.

Several limitations should be considered. The cross-sectional design precluded establishing temporality and limits causal interpretation; residual confounding and reverse causation remain possible. The limited survey design degrees of freedom necessitated the collapsing of race/ethnicity and education categories, reducing the detail with which these characteristics could be represented. Antihypertensive medication use was not included in the primary regression models; consequently, the estimated associations reflect measured BP without adjustment for current treatment status, which may influence observed BP levels and associations with other characteristics. Predictive performance was modest, and subgroup performance estimates may have been affected by differences in subgroup size. Although cross-validation and a held-out test set provided internal evaluation, external validation in independent data was not performed, and the models’ generalizability to other populations remains uncertain. Therefore, the predictive results do not establish generalizability to independent populations or readiness for clinical implementation.

Overall, the study demonstrates that characteristics associated with BP at the population level do not necessarily provide accurate individual-level predictions. The selected predictors captured some variation in SBP and DBP, but substantial individual-level variation remained unexplained. Further improvements may require accounting for nonlinear relationships like using restricted cubic splines and investigating a limited number of interactions. The findings should therefore be viewed as a characterization of adjusted associations and internally evaluated predictive performance, rather than evidence of causal effects or established clinical utility.
